text: A finance team's expense table has been locked down by strict field-level ACLs for three years running. The analysts who need that data every single day don't have the role required to see it — so every week, one of the handful of people who do have that role exports the entire table, override field included, to a spreadsheet with absolutely no audit trail at all.

Step one is going field by field and asking which ones are genuinely sensitive versus which ones were simply swept into the same blanket restriction three years ago without that question ever being asked. Four fields — amount, cost center, vendor, and approval notes — turn out to be needed daily and carry no special risk. Only the approval-chain override field is genuinely sensitive enough to justify staying locked down.

Step two is creating a new finance_analyst role scoped specifically to exactly those four fields analysts actually use, while leaving the override field's existing finance_admin-only ACL completely untouched. That one targeted change removes the reason the weekly export ever existed in the first place, with proper per-user audit logging automatically restored on every single access going forward.

Step three is retiring the workaround deliberately, not just assuming it stops on its own. Disable the scheduled export job, notify the finance team that in-platform access now genuinely covers their daily work, and then check back in a few weeks to confirm the ad hoc export requests have actually stopped — not merely that the new role was technically created and deployed.

If a brand-new export request shows up weeks later anyway, that's a clear signal some analyst still needs a field the finance_analyst role doesn't currently cover. The right response is revisiting the role definition itself, not assuming the fix is finished simply because it already shipped and looked complete on paper.

Strict exactly where risk justifies it, and genuinely frictionless everywhere else — and the real proof it worked is a workaround that quietly disappears, not a policy memo nobody reads. Chapter 5 is now complete. Next, Chapter 6 opens with architecting for performance at scale, as an instance's data volume and user traffic keep growing year over year.
